Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Interior Designer
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Anniversaries: The anniversary of the event, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events
  Maladaptive Strategies: Worst Case Rehearsal: mentally rehearse worst case scenarios to feel prepared, Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively

Vignette:
Vikram Patel was thirty-nine when the phone rang on a Tuesday in late October, delivering news that his younger brother had collapsed during a morning run and was gone before the ambulance arrived. The suddenness of it lodged in him immediately, not as a story he would later tell, but as a physical weight. He had come to believe that death could arrive without warning, without a season or a symptom to prepare him. Within the first month, his body began reacting to danger before his mind had time to catch up. A sudden door slam or the sharp crack of a car backfiring would tighten his shoulders and quicken his pulse, leaving him standing in a grocery aisle or sitting in his client’s living room, already braced. The feeling was so visceral that he sometimes forgot he was safe until his breathing settled. When the memories surfaced, they did not arrive as quiet reflections but as brief returns; he would catch himself looking at his wife with the same startled recognition he felt on that October day, as though the moment were happening again right now. As the calendar turned, Vikram’s responses took shape into patterns he no longer questioned. Because his brother had been gone without a season or a warning, anniversaries felt less like milestones and more like mirrors, and he avoided them not out of sentiment but out of habit. He avoided funerals, cemeteries, and any gathering where people spoke about loss. A conversation about a neighbor’s passing or a client mentioning a parent’s illness would send him quietly out of the room or into his studio, where he could watch floor plans and material swatches without having to listen. Worst-case rehearsal became a nightly habit; he would lie beside his wife and mentally walk through scenarios, preparing himself for the next unexpected turn, as though readiness could soften the impact. His irritability surfaced in quiet ways—a sharp tone when his wife asked about plans, a sudden frustration when a contractor delayed a delivery, a tendency to snap over small interruptions that felt suddenly significant. These reactions did not follow one another so much as they accumulated, layering over his days like familiar routines. His work as an interior designer provided the daily stage where these habits played out. While inspecting a client’s mid-century home in late October, Vikram stood in a sunlit kitchen, measuring a new island, when a delivery cart rattled past the open door. His chest tightened before he registered the sound, and for a few seconds he was back in the hospital corridor, watching the same unspooling of time he had witnessed with his brother. He had learned to recognize the familiar shift, and he stepped outside, telling his client he needed to check the lighting samples in the showroom. He avoided the floral arrangements in the waiting area, preferring the clean lines of steel and glass that felt predictable. The avoidance had real consequences: he missed a firm anniversary gathering, and his wife noticed how he seemed physically present but mentally distant, as though he were conserving his attention for whatever might arrive. His irritable moments had made him withdraw from casual dinners, and his worst-case rehearsals had made him double-book appointments, as though preparation were a form of control. Vikram had come to see his days as a series of manageable distances, carefully measured against the calendar and the quiet risks of the house. He sought help now because the narrowing of his routines had begun to feel less like protection and more like absence, and because the sudden physical surges left him exhausted by midday. He was most afraid of being caught unprepared when another unexpected loss arrived, and he hoped simply to walk through an anniversary without bracing, to listen to stories about grief without turning away, and to let his body and mind meet in the same moment.
